newsitem.title: USA: Convicted bomber could face death in Alabama.
newsitem.headline: Convicted bomber could face death in Alabama.

text.p: The man who masterminded a 1989 wave of mail bombings in the South faced a possible death sentence Monday for the murder of a federal judge in Alabama.
Walter Leroy Moody Jr., whose deadly bombing campaign raised racial tensions in three Southern states, was due to appear for sentencing at 9:30 a.m. EST in Jefferson County Circuit Court.

An Alabama jury in November convicted the 61-year-old for the 1989 slaying of 11th U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Vance, who died while opening a package containing a bomb in his Mountain Brook home. The judge's wife, Helen Vance, was injured in the blast.
The same jury of nine women and three men later recommended the death penalty to Judge William Rhea of Etowah County.
Bob Morrow, the chief prosecutor at Moody's trial, said any sentence amounting to less than death in the Alabama electric chair -- known to prison officials as "Yellow Mama" -- would be unacceptable.
"I hope we send a message out to anybody that thinks they're going to come to Alabama and bomb people that they will get the death penalty," Morrow said.

At the time of his state conviction, Moody already was serving life without parole on federal charges stemming from the murders of Vance and black civil rights attorney Robert Robinson in Savannah, Ga.
Prosecutors say Moody mailed out a total of four bombs from August to December 1989 after becoming frustrated by his own inability to overturn a 1972 conviction for possessing a pipe bomb.
The bomb that killed Robinson in December 1989 was meant to make police think a white supremacist group, such as the Ku Klux Klan, was behind the Vance murder.

Moody also mailed a bomb to the Jacksonville, Fla., office of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People. But it was intercepted, along with a fourth device sent to the offices of the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta.
The convicted bomber, who was not represented by an attorney in November, presented no defence at his trial as his behaviour swung between angry outbursts and quiet torpor.

During the proceedings, Moody's ex-wife testified that she bought the cardboard boxes, flashlight batteries, bulbs, aluminum pie plates, mailing packets and labels used to package the bomb that killed Vance.
A former girlfriend also told jurors how Moody had talked about a bombing as the perfect crime.
In 1990, the FBI bugged Moody's house and soon was able to record him muttering to himself. At one point, he made a muttered reference to two fatal bombings.
